files.codex/u1-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Taking an Argument Apart
1. "Our district should move the middle school start time to 8:45."
2. Health (students need more sleep than an early start allows) and learning (tired students learn less).
3. Health: sleep doctors' recommended hours, the body clock shifting later during puberty, and the arithmetic of sleeping at eleven and waking at six (seven hours at most). Learning: the student council survey, in which 64 percent of 212 eighth graders said they had fallen or nearly fallen asleep in a morning class.
4. A later start could make sports and jobs end late, and families who leave early for work would have nowhere to send their children.
5. Strength: it surveys many students at this school, and it measures something connected to learning. Weakness: it is self-reported, the questions and sampling are not described, and falling asleep in class is not the same as learning less. Accept any reasonable strength and weakness.
6. The library opens at 7:00 for early arrivals and practices could move to the lit gym. Accept either judgment if it is explained, for example that the rebuttal answers child care but not students with after-school jobs.

Phones in the Classroom (writing task)
Look for: a claim in one sentence on either side; two distinct reasons, each with specific evidence (an example, a fact, a survey, an expert's view); a counterclaim stated fairly; a rebuttal that actually answers it; at least 250 words. Either position can earn Advanced. A strong rebuttal concedes something true before answering it.

Is It Ever Right to Break a Promise? (writing task and discussion)
Look for: a clear position, one reason with a specific example, an objection a thoughtful classmate would really make, a reply to that objection, and two sentences of reflection that name a classmate's idea. In the discussion, students should name the strongest part of an opposing view before replying.

Evaluate an Argument
1. The school board should ban homework completely, starting next month.
2. No. One example cannot prove a general rule (a hasty generalization), and the cousin may be smart for reasons that have nothing to do with homework.
3. No. Five friends who eat lunch with the writer are a tiny, likely like-minded sample. "Everyone" is an overstatement that the evidence cannot support.
4. The pizza party paragraph is irrelevant: whether students enjoy pizza parties says nothing about whether homework helps them practice. Accept also the water cycle worksheet if the student argues one boring assignment is not about homework in general, though it is better described as insufficient than irrelevant.
5. The best answer is usually the last reason (students need time to rest and be with family), because it names a real cost that applies to many students, though it still needs evidence. Accept another choice if it is well explained.
6. Example: "Some people argue that homework is a waste of time. It is true that some assignments repeat what students already know. However, practice spread over several days helps people remember what they learn, and homework is often the only time a student practices alone, without a teacher or classmate to lean on."

Scoring tip: in the assessment, the reasoning and relevance criteria reward naming the flaw (one example, a small sample, an unrelated fact) more than labeling it with a technical term. A student who says "one cousin is not enough to prove anything about all students" has the idea and can earn Proficient.",
  "id": "u1-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Argument Writing",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u1-overview.json:
{
  "body": "An argument is not a fight. It is a way of explaining what you think and why a fair-minded reader should agree.

Every strong argument has five parts:
1. Claim: your position in one clear sentence.
2. Reasons: why a reader should agree.
3. Evidence: facts, data, examples or expert quotes for each reason.
4. Counterclaim: the strongest objection, stated fairly.
5. Rebuttal: why your claim still holds.

In this unit you will take apart a student's argument for a later school start, write your own argument about phones in class, discuss whether it is ever right to break a promise, and finish by judging whether another writer's reasons and evidence really support his claim.

Ask yourself as you read and write: is this evidence relevant? Is there enough of it? Would someone who disagrees find it fair?",
  "id": "u1-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Claims, Reasons and Counterclaims",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u1-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students write an argument that introduces a claim, supports it with clear reasons and relevant evidence, and acknowledges and answers an opposing claim (W.8.1).
- Students trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, judging whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence relevant and sufficient, and recognizing irrelevant evidence (RI.8.8).
- Students take part in a collaborative discussion, posing questions and responding to others' ideas with relevant evidence (SL.8.1).

MATERIALS
- The student overview, projected, with the five parts of an argument
- "Let Us Sleep" (the passage in Taking an Argument Apart)
- Five highlighter colors or digital highlights: claim, reasons, evidence, counterclaim, rebuttal
- An argument planner: claim, reason 1 with evidence, reason 2 with evidence, counterclaim, rebuttal
- "Ban Homework Now" (the letter in the assessment), kept back until Day 5

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read the overview together. Ask students to argue for 30 seconds, with a partner, about a low-stakes question (best season, best pizza topping). Then name which of the five parts they used. Most will have a claim and a reason; few will have a counterclaim.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Taking an Argument Apart. Read "Let Us Sleep" aloud and color-code its parts as a class before students answer. Discuss question 5: is a student council survey strong evidence?
Day 3: Assign Phones in the Classroom. Students fill in the planner, then draft. Model a rebuttal that is fair to the other side: "Some people argue... This is a real concern. However..."
Day 4: Peer review of phones drafts: partners highlight the claim and the counterclaim and write one question about the evidence. Then students write Breaking a Promise and discuss it in groups of four, naming the strongest point of someone who disagrees before replying.
Day 5: Assessment: Evaluate an Argument. Students read "Ban Homework Now" on their own and answer without AI help. Collect phones final drafts by the due date.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give students the planner with sentence starters ("I believe...", "One reason is...", "For example...", "Some people argue...", "However..."). Let them write the phones argument at 150 words first, then extend.
- Support: in the lesson, pre-highlight the claim so students start by finding reasons.
- Stretch: ask students to find a second counterclaim for the phones argument and decide which one is stronger, and to add a source they find with an adult's help.
- Multilingual learners: preteach claim, evidence, counterclaim and rebuttal with a visual (a courtroom: the lawyer's claim, the exhibits, the other side, the answer). Allow planning notes in the home language; the final draft is in English.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit your child is learning to write arguments: a clear claim, reasons and evidence, and a fair answer to the other side. They will write about whether students should keep phones in class. At dinner, try a friendly debate on a small question (should dessert come before dinner on weekends?). Ask your child to state the other side's best point before answering it. That one habit is the heart of good argument.",
  "id": "u1-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Argument Writing",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u2-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Tracing a Theme ("The Second Key")
1. Independence and being trusted ("You're old enough now"), but also being alone: it lets her into an empty kitchen and a silent hallway.
2. She is wrapped up in her own loneliness ("her own key and her own silence to deal with"); she does not yet see that Teo feels the same way.
3. She invites Teo in to share the snack. Her own experience of the empty kitchen helps her understand how he feels waiting alone.
4. The second note says "Enough for two" and comes with a second key: her mother approves and makes the kindness lasting. The repeated note shows the change from a lonely routine to a shared one.
5. Examples: "Sharing what you have can turn loneliness into belonging." "People who know what it is like to be alone are often the first to notice someone else who is."
6. Strong choices: "It's usually enough for two" or Marisol's note "For days you forget. Or for days you just don't want to sit on the stairs," with an explanation linking it to the theme.

Theme in "The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter" (writing task)
Likely themes: courage is acting in spite of fear, not the absence of it; people discover their strength when someone needs them. Look for development across the story: the beginning (Nell afraid of the stairs and pretending not to care), the turning point (the storm, her shaking hands, counting the steps as her father did) and the end ("Nell did not feel brave... Maybe, she thought, that was the point"). At least two passages, each explained, not just quoted; at least 300 words.

Theme Check ("The Paper Cranes")
1. He wants his grandmother to get well; a book said folding a thousand cranes may grant a wish.
2. He cares only about reaching the number, as if the wish were a rule to satisfy; he is focused on the goal, not the people or the process.
3. She joins him; folding together becomes time spent together and opens her stories about her childhood, so the cranes become about their time, not the count.
4. He has stopped focusing on the outcome and started valuing the time with his grandmother.
5. Examples: "The time we spend with people we love can matter more than the result we hope for." "Love is found in shared effort more than in perfect results."
6. Look for the beginning (counting, the wish), a middle passage (the crooked crane, "Look how you learned," the evenings of stories) and the end (forgetting the wish, deciding it was already granted).

Scoring tip: a theme stated as a single word ("love") or as a plot summary is Developing on the theme criterion. Proficient needs a full sentence about life that the whole story supports, including the ending.",
  "id": "u2-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Theme in Short Fiction",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u2-overview.json:
{
  "body": "A theme is a message about life that a story suggests. It is rarely stated. Instead, the writer lets it grow through the story, and a careful reader traces it.

To trace a theme, watch:
- what characters want and what they do,
- how the conflict changes them,
- objects or images that repeat.

A topic is one word (courage, loneliness). A theme is a full sentence that says something about the topic: "Courage is acting even when you are afraid."

Our story: "The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter." We will also read "The Second Key" and "The Paper Cranes." For each one, ask: what does the main character believe at the start, and what do they understand by the end?",
  "id": "u2-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Reading for Theme",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u2-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students determine a theme of a story and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to the characters, setting and plot (RL.8.2).
- Students cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports their analysis (RL.8.1).
- Students analyze how particular lines of dialogue or incidents propel the action and reveal aspects of a character (RL.8.3).

MATERIALS
- "The Second Key" (in the lesson activity) and "The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter" (the reading for the writing task), printed for annotation
- A theme tracker: beginning, middle, end columns with rows for wants, actions, change and repeated images
- Chart paper with the frame "[Topic] is... / Sometimes people... / The story suggests that..."
- "The Paper Cranes" (in the assessment), kept back until Day 5

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read the overview. Contrast topic and theme with three examples from movies students know. Read "The Second Key" aloud and fill in the theme tracker together for the beginning.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Tracing a Theme. Students finish the tracker in pairs, then answer the questions. Share theme statements and test each against the ending: does the ending support it?
Day 3: Read "The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter" twice: once for the story, once with the tracker. Assign the literary analysis. Model choosing two passages, one early and one late, that show the theme changing.
Day 4: Writing workshop on the analysis. Mini-lesson on introducing and explaining a quotation (set it up, quote it, explain what it shows about the theme).
Day 5: Assessment: Theme Check. Students read "The Paper Cranes" independently and answer without AI help. The analysis draft continues toward its due date.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a partly completed tracker for "The Second Key" and a bank of possible topics (loneliness, kindness, belonging, courage). Students choose a topic, then turn it into a theme sentence with the frame.
- Support: for the analysis, allow a five-paragraph scaffold: theme, early passage, middle passage, late passage, conclusion.
- Stretch: ask students to argue for a second theme in the same story and explain which is better supported, or to analyze how a repeated image (the stairs, the key, the cranes) carries the theme.
- Multilingual learners: preteach story vocabulary (spiral, mainland, railing; refrigerator note, hook; lopsided, granted) with pictures. Pair students to read aloud before writing, and accept a theme statement drafted in the home language and then translated together.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit we are reading short stories for theme: the message about life a story suggests without saying it outright. Ask your child about "The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter": what was Nell afraid of, and what did she learn? Then try it with a movie or show you watch together. What does the main character want at the start, and what do they understand by the end?",
  "id": "u2-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Theme in Short Fiction",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u3-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "How a Memoir Works
1. "The wind roared in my ears" (hearing, touch); "the cracks in the road blurred into one gray stripe" (sight). Accept any two with the senses named.
2. Crashes happen in an instant; the short sentence mirrors the suddenness. It also shows that the crash is not the point of the story; the repair is.
3. He believes in the writer and wants the writer to learn, not just to have the bike fixed. The writer points it out because it is the turning point: the grandfather gives responsibility instead of rescue.
4. The final paragraph. The adult understands that the grandfather was teaching patience and that a broken thing is not the end of the story; at eleven, the writer thought he was being stubborn.
5. To share a lesson about patience and repair learned from a grandfather. Supporting quotation: "a broken thing is not the end of the story, if you are willing to be patient with it, and with yourself."

Snapshot and Thoughtshot
Look for: a moment under a minute, told in slow motion; details from at least three senses; one line of dialogue in quotation marks; a separate reflective paragraph in the present-day voice ("Now I understand..."). At least 150 words.

My Memoir
Look for: an opening that sets place and time and draws the reader in; events in a clear order with transitions; the key moment slowed down with dialogue and description; a conclusion that reflects rather than simply ends; a note on the biggest revision. At least 400 words. Content is the student's own choice; do not grade the significance of the event, only how it is told.

Reading a Memoir
1. As a child, the writer thought the radio simply belonged to the mother like her glasses. At twelve, the writer learned it was the only thing she brought from her homeland and that it sometimes picked up a broadcast in her first language.
2. The voices fade in and out of the static, surfacing briefly the way swimmers surface; it suggests struggle and distance, a far-off home reaching her only in pieces.
3. The writer respects the mother's private moment of longing for home; it shows understanding and tenderness, not embarrassment.
4. From embarrassment ("I turned it off" when friends came over) to love and connection (the writer keeps a radio and sometimes listens to static "for the swimmers").
5. To show how the writer came to understand and honor a parent's loss and heritage. The last sentence shows the writer now shares the mother's habit and listens for what she listened for, so the meaning has been inherited.

Scoring tip: on the reflection criterion, a conclusion that only says "I learned my lesson" is Developing. Proficient reflection says what the lesson was and how the writer sees the moment differently now.",
  "id": "u3-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Memoir and Personal Narrative",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u3-overview.json:
{
  "body": "A memoir is a true story from the writer's own life. It is not a whole autobiography. It zooms in on one moment, or one summer, and asks: what did this mean?

Memoir writers use the tools of fiction:
- dialogue, to let people speak for themselves,
- pacing, slowing down the most important seconds and skipping the boring hours,
- sensory detail, so the reader sees, hears and feels the moment,
- and reflection: the older writer looking back and explaining what the younger self did not yet understand.

This unit we read two memoir excerpts, "The Summer of the Broken Bicycle" and "The Radio on the Windowsill." Then you will write your own memoir about a moment that changed you. You choose what to share; it does not need to be dramatic. A broken bicycle can be enough.",
  "id": "u3-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Small Moments, Big Meanings",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u3-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students write a narrative of a real experience using dialogue, pacing, description and reflection, with a logical sequence of events and a conclusion that reflects on what was experienced (W.8.3).
- Students determine an author's point of view or purpose in a memoir and analyze how the author develops it (RI.8.6).
- Students cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports their analysis of a memoir (RI.8.1).
- Students develop and strengthen their writing by planning, revising and editing, with help from peers (W.8.5).

MATERIALS
- "The Summer of the Broken Bicycle" (in the lesson activity), printed for annotation
- A technique chart: dialogue, pacing (slow-motion moments), sensory detail, reflection
- Timeline planner for the memoir: before, the moment (in slow motion), after, what I understand now
- "The Radio on the Windowsill" (in the assessment), kept back until Day 5

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read the overview. Students list five small moments they remember clearly (a lost tooth, a first day, a fall, a win, a goodbye). Read "The Summer of the Broken Bicycle" aloud.
Day 2: Lesson activity: How a Memoir Works. Students find each technique on the chart in the bicycle excerpt. Discuss: why does the race take one paragraph but the repair take a month and a paragraph too?
Day 3: Snapshot and Thoughtshot. Students write one moment in slow motion with sensory detail, then a reflection. Share in pairs; partners point to the strongest sensory detail.
Day 4: Students choose their memoir moment, fill in the timeline planner and draft My Memoir. Peer conference: the partner asks two questions the draft does not yet answer.
Day 5: Assessment: Reading a Memoir. Students read "The Radio on the Windowsill" on their own and answer without AI help. Memoirs continue through revision to their due date.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: offer a list of moment prompts (a time you were surprised, a time you learned something from an older person, a time something went wrong) and the timeline planner with sentence starters for reflection ("At the time I thought... Now I understand...").
- Support: allow a memoir of 250 words with a clear beginning, slow-motion middle and reflective ending.
- Stretch: ask students to use a repeated object or image (like the radio) to carry the meaning, or to write the ending reflection without stating the lesson directly.
- Multilingual learners: invite students to include a word or phrase in their home language where it is true to the memory, with meaning clear from context. Provide a bank of sensory verbs and adjectives.
- Some memories are painful. Remind students they choose what to share, and that a small, ordinary moment makes a fine memoir.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit your child is writing a memoir: a true story about one moment from their life and what it meant. Family stories can help. Tell your child about a moment you remember from when you were their age, and ask them which moments they remember most clearly. They choose what to write about and what to share.",
  "id": "u3-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Memoir and Personal Narrative",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u4-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Finding the Central Idea
1. Bringing a buried creek back into the open air (in Millbrook, removing a parking lot over a creek that had run in a pipe).
2. Example: Uncovering Fenner Creek improved Millbrook's downtown by reducing flooding, cooling the area, bringing back wildlife and helping businesses.
3. Flooding: four street floods in five years after, eleven in five years before. Temperature and wildlife: about 2 degrees Celsius cooler on summer afternoons; three fish species. Business: 24 of 31 shops reported more customers; rents rose about 18 percent.
4. A pipe can carry only so much water before it backs up; an open creek with planted banks spreads out and lets water soak into the ground.
5. Example: Millbrook removed a parking lot in 2019 to uncover Fenner Creek, which had run in a pipe since the 1940s. A city report says the three-year, $14 million project reduced flooding, cooled the area and brought back fish. Most shops along the creek also reported more customers.

Where the Sources Disagree
Disagreements students should find: (a) rents: the report says about 18 percent (for shops); the letter says close to 30 percent for apartments, because the report measured store rents, not home rents; (b) business success: the report says 24 of 31 shops gained customers; the letter says four original shops closed during construction and were not surveyed. Also accept a disagreement of interpretation: success for the city versus displacement of residents. Look for both sources quoted, an explanation of why (different measurements, who was counted, each writer's purpose) and a conclusion about what a reader needs to know. At least 300 words.

Explain a Local Change
Look for: a focused, answerable question; at least three sources of more than one kind; a credibility note on one rejected source; organized sections with transitions; facts, quotations and examples; paraphrase in the student's own words; a source list with author, title, date and location. At least 500 words. Check a sample of quotations against the sources the student lists.

Informational Reading Check
1. Not letting water pass through or soak in; context: "water runs off them instead of soaking in."
2. Example: Rain gardens are a cheap, natural way for schools to catch runoff, reduce flooding and pollution, and create habitat, though they are not a cure for every problem.
3. Runoff flows into the shallow garden; water pools for a day or two; it slowly soaks into the soil; the soil filters out pollutants; the water reaches the groundwater; native roots keep the soil loose to absorb more.
4. They give a real, specific example and numbers (about 90,000 liters a month from one roof) that show the size of the problem and that the solution worked (the puddle is gone).
5. It turns from benefits to limits (weeding, soil that drains well). It makes the article balanced and more credible.
6. A summary should name the problem (runoff from impervious surfaces), the solution (rain gardens and how they work), the example, and the limits, with no opinion.

Scoring tip: for Where the Sources Disagree, the explanation criterion is the heart of the task. Proficient work says why the numbers differ (they measured different things or counted different people), not only that they differ.",
  "id": "u4-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Informational Reading and Research",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u4-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Researchers do not just collect facts. They ask a question, read several sources, notice where the sources agree and disagree, and then explain what they found in their own words, giving credit to every source.

In this unit you will:
- find the central idea of an article and how it is developed,
- compare two texts about the same project that give conflicting information, and decide why they disagree,
- research a question about a change in your own community, and write an explanatory report with at least three sources.

Our sources are about Millbrook, an invented city that uncovered a creek buried under a parking lot. The articles are written for this course, but cities around the world have really done this.

Keep asking: who wrote this? What did they measure, and what did they leave out?",
  "id": "u4-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Reading Like a Researcher",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u4-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students determine a central idea of an informational text and analyze its development, including its relationship to supporting ideas (RI.8.2).
- Students cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports their analysis (RI.8.1).
- Students analyze a case in which two texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation (RI.8.9).
- Students write an informative text that examines a topic with relevant facts, quotations and examples, precise vocabulary and a formal style (W.8.2).
- Students conduct a short research project on a question, drawing on several sources (W.8.7), and gather and quote information from sources while assessing their credibility and avoiding plagiarism, with a basic citation format (W.8.8).
- Students determine the meaning of technical words in an article and analyze how a paragraph's structure develops a key concept (RI.8.4, RI.8.5).

MATERIALS
- "Opening the Creek" (the lesson passage and a reading) and "A Creek for Whom?" (a reading), printed side by side
- A two-column comparison organizer: what Source A says, what Source B says, why they differ
- A research log: question, source, author, date, credibility notes, key facts, quotation with page or paragraph
- A one-page citation guide in the school's chosen format
- Library or classroom access for community research (local news archives, city websites, interviews with adults)
- "Why Some Schools Are Digging Up Their Lawns" (in the assessment), kept back until Day 5

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read the overview. Lesson activity: Finding the Central Idea in "Opening the Creek." Model separating the central idea from supporting details.
Day 2: Read "A Creek for Whom?" Complete the comparison organizer in pairs, then assign Where the Sources Disagree. Discuss: does one source lie, or do they measure different things?
Day 3: Launch Explain a Local Change. Students brainstorm changes in their community (a new park, a closed store, a bike lane) and write a research question. Mini-lesson on judging credibility: who wrote it, why, how they know.
Day 4: Research workshop. Students fill in the research log with at least three sources and practise paraphrasing versus quoting. Check every log for a source and a credibility note.
Day 5: Assessment: Informational Reading Check. Students read the rain gardens article on their own and answer without AI help. Research reports continue to their due date over the next two weeks.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a sentence-level paraphrasing practice set and a report outline (introduction with the question, two or three body sections each built on a source, conclusion). Allow two sources plus one interview.
- Support: offer a short list of pre-approved community questions and sources for students who struggle to start.
- Stretch: ask students to find a source that disagrees with their others and explain the disagreement in the report, as in Where the Sources Disagree.
- Multilingual learners: preteach the domain words (impervious, runoff, daylighting, rent, survey) with images. Allow sources in the home language when students paraphrase them into English and cite them.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit your child is learning to research like a professional: asking a question, reading several sources, and noticing when sources disagree. Their project is a report on a change in our community. You can help by talking about a change you have noticed (a new building, a business that closed, a road that changed) and, if you can, by being a source they interview.",
  "id": "u4-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Informational Reading and Research",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u5-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Reading a Poem Closely
1. The cold shuts the kids out and keeps them from comfort; they are stuck, powerless, waiting for something to let them in.
2. "stamping our boots like impatient horses" (the kids' restless feet and horses pawing the ground); "the color of a nickel / someone left in the rain" (the gray sky and a dull, tarnished coin); "yellow as a struck match" (the bus and a flame). Accept any one with both parts named.
3. Short, clipped sentences mirror the kids saving their energy; the mood is tight, silent and frozen.
4. From cold, gray and still to warm, bright and hopeful, at "Then the bus turns the corner, / yellow as a struck match."
5. Sunflowers turn toward the sun without thinking; the kids lean toward the bus the same way. It suggests the bus is like the sun: warmth, light and relief.

Two Poems, Two Shapes
Dickinson: hope is a small bird that lives in the soul, sings without words, never stops, is sweetest in the storm and never asks for anything. The form is three regular quatrains with a hymn-like rhythm and slant rhyme; the dashes create pauses that feel like breath or birdsong, and the steady pattern mirrors hope's constancy. The Tuesday poem: it openly rejects the bird and compares hope to a clanking basement furnace that catches after a moment of doubt; hope is ordinary, mechanical and learned from a parent. Its short, broken free-verse lines ("listening, / not sure, / and then") slow the reader into the speaker's uncertain waiting, and the ending instruction ("you can stop waiting / and get up") makes hope practical. Look for both metaphors explained, a real comparison of structures with effects, two quotations from each poem, at least 350 words.

My Extended Metaphor Poem
Look for: one comparison sustained through at least 12 lines, not dropped after the first stanza; at least two concrete images; one named sound device; line breaks that do something (emphasis, pause, surprise); an author's note of about 100 words naming the metaphor and one choice about form.

Poetry Check
1. A wooden spoon; not silver or land. Opening with what was not left sets up a surprise: the inheritance seems small but turns out to be precious.
2. She cooked with it every day for a lifetime, in the same way; it shows routine, care and long love for her family.
3. Personification (the wood waiting). It suggests the spoon recognizes the speaker as part of the family, that the habit and the love have passed on.
4. The break makes the reader pause on "only," then land on "by using them," so the final idea arrives with emphasis and surprise.
5. Example: "Some of what we inherit from people we love is kept alive only by practising it." The last stanza contrasts things kept in a drawer with things inherited by use, turning the spoon into a symbol of a living tradition.

Scoring tip: on the structure criterion, naming a feature ("it has three stanzas") without its effect is Developing. Proficient explains what the feature does to the reading or the meaning.",

{
  "body": "A poem says a lot in a small space, so every word has to work. Poets choose words for their sound as well as their meaning, build images you can see, and arrange lines and stanzas so the shape of the poem helps say what it means.

Tools to look for:
- simile and metaphor: comparisons, with or without like or as,
- extended metaphor: one comparison carried through a whole poem,
- tone: the speaker's attitude, shown through word choice,
- form: line breaks, stanzas, rhyme and rhythm, or the lack of them.

We will read original poems written for this course and one poem written about 160 years ago by Emily Dickinson. Then you will write your own.

Read every poem at least twice, once aloud.",

files.codex/u5-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students determine the meaning of words and phrases in poems, including figurative and connotative meanings, and analyze the impact of word choice on meaning and tone (RL.8.4).
- Students compare and contrast the structure of two poems and analyze how each structure contributes to its meaning and style (RL.8.5).
- Students determine a theme of a poem and analyze its development (RL.8.2).
- Students interpret figures of speech in context and use them in their own writing (L.8.5).

MATERIALS
- "Bus Stop, January" (in the lesson activity), printed with wide margins
- "Hope" is the thing with feathers, by Emily Dickinson (public domain), and "What Hope Sounds Like on a Tuesday" (readings for the comparison)
- A form chart: line length, stanzas, rhyme, rhythm, punctuation, and what each does to the reading
- Colored pencils for marking images, sound devices and shifts in tone
- "Inheritance" (in the assessment), kept back until Day 5

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read the overview. Read "Bus Stop, January" aloud twice. Lesson activity: Reading a Poem Closely. Students mark each comparison and the moment the tone changes.
Day 2: Read Dickinson's poem aloud. Note its hymn-like rhythm, its quatrains, its dashes and its single extended metaphor. Read "What Hope Sounds Like on a Tuesday" and fill in the form chart for both.
Day 3: Assign Two Poems, Two Shapes. Model one paragraph: how the short, broken lines of the furnace poem slow the reader down to listen, the way the speaker does.
Day 4: Writing workshop. Students brainstorm an abstract idea (patience, home, worry, friendship) and an everyday object to compare it to, then draft My Extended Metaphor. Poetry read-around: each student reads two lines aloud.
Day 5: Assessment: Poetry Check. Students read "Inheritance" on their own and answer without AI help.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a glossary for the Dickinson poem (perches, gale, abash, extremity) and read it aloud more than once. Offer a comparison frame: "Poem A uses ___, which makes the reader ___. Poem B uses ___, which ___."
- Support: for the poem, offer a template: "[Idea] is a [object]. It ___. It ___. When ___, it ___." and allow 8 lines.
- Stretch: ask students to write their poem in a fixed form (quatrains with a regular rhyme scheme) and explain how the form fits the subject, or to write two versions in different forms.
- Multilingual learners: poems are a good place to bring home languages in. Invite students to share a proverb or poem from another language that uses a metaphor, and to explain it. Pre-teach the idea of connotation with word pairs (cheap and inexpensive).

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit we are reading and writing poetry. We are reading a famous poem by Emily Dickinson that compares hope to a bird, and your child will write a poem that compares an idea to an everyday object. Ask your child to read you their poem aloud. You might also share a song lyric, saying or poem from your family or culture and talk about what it compares.",
  "id": "u5-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Poetry: Image, Sound and Form",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u6-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Reading a Script
1. That Anika broke the volcano (it fell when she tried to make it erupt). The playwright uses an aside, Anika speaking directly to the audience, and a stage direction showing the broken volcano hidden under the towel.
2. To keep Dev from lifting the towel; it shows she is guilty and panicking, and it makes the audience tense.
3. Examples: "The science fair bus leaves at eight" (a time limit); "If I don't have it, I have nothing... a third of our grade" (the cost of losing it).
4. Dev says hiding was worse than breaking; it shows Anika what her hiding will feel like and that Dev understands mistakes, so she steps off the towel and confesses.
5. Accept either answer if supported. Many students will argue he suspects her: her "too quick" answer, his quiet tone, and his choosing that story at that moment. Others will argue he is only explaining how he feels.

Readers' Theater
Look for: a complete recorded performance in which lines are delivered with expression and pauses that fit the character; a reasoned choice for Dev's phone story (for example, quiet and slow, to make it feel like a confession); physical acting for Anika (glancing at the towel, standing on it); a real disagreement and how it was solved; a specific improvement. Score delivery and interpretation from the recording, collaboration from your observation during rehearsal.

Dramatic Irony in "The Volcano"
Look for: a claim that the audience's knowledge of the hidden volcano creates both suspense (will Dev find it, will Anika confess before the bus) and humor ("What volcano?", "Maybe Mom moved it", "explain volcanoes with your hands"); at least two quoted moments with explanation; the gap closing when Anika lifts the towel; why her confession matters (it shows her choosing honesty, prompted by Dev's story, and makes the ending about forgiveness instead of being caught). At least 300 words.

Drama Check
1. That she calmed a frightened dog in the hallway, so she already has a gift for working with nervous animals.
2. Carmen is nervous and saying what she thinks interviewers want to hear; Mr. Okafor is unimpressed and writes nothing, showing he wants something real.
3. The audience knows Carmen is good with animals, so we worry her honest answer will cost her the job even though it is unfair.
4. Pepper's frantic barking and Carmen's offer to try something; it gives her the chance to show, not tell, and leads to Mr. Okafor writing her down.
5. That he is impressed and is likely to hire her.
6. He repeats her earlier weakness ironically: she has no formal experience but clearly knows what she is doing, so the phrase now means the opposite of what it meant before.

Scoring tip: on the irony criterion, Proficient answers say what the audience knows, what the character does not, and the effect (tension or humor). Naming "dramatic irony" without the effect is Developing.",
  "id": "u6-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Drama: Dialogue and Point of View",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u6-overview.json:
{
  "body": "A play is written to be performed. The script holds two kinds of text: dialogue, which the characters speak, and stage directions, in parentheses, which tell the actors what to do and the audience what to see.\n\nIn a play, nobody explains what a character is thinking. You learn about characters from what they say, what they do, and what they hide.\n\nPlaywrights love dramatic irony: when the audience knows something a character does not. Watching a character walk right past the answer is tense, or funny, or both.\n\nThis unit we read two original scenes, \"The Volcano\" and \"The Interview.\" In small groups you will rehearse and perform \"The Volcano\" as readers' theater, then write about how its dramatic irony works.",
  "id": "u6-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "When the Audience Knows More",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u6-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students analyze how particular lines of dialogue or incidents in a drama propel the action, reveal aspects of a character, or provoke a decision (RL.8.3).
- Students analyze how differences in the points of view of the characters and the audience create suspense or humor (RL.8.6).
- Students engage in collaborative discussions and rehearsals, building on others' ideas and following agreed-upon rules for group work (SL.8.1).
- Students adapt their speech to a dramatic performance, using volume, pace and expression appropriate to the character (SL.8.6).

MATERIALS
- "The Volcano" (in the lesson activity and readings), one copy per student for marking
- Highlighters in two colors: what the audience knows, what Dev knows
- A rehearsal role card: director, Dev, Anika, Mom and stage directions reader
- A space to perform, and devices to record groups
- "The Interview" (in the assessment), kept back until Day 5

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read the overview. Explain stage directions and asides. Lesson activity: Reading a Script. Read "The Volcano" aloud with volunteers, then students answer.
Day 2: Teach dramatic irony with a quick example. Students highlight what the audience knows and what Dev knows in two colors. Assign Dramatic Irony in "The Volcano."
Day 3: Readers' theater rehearsal. Groups assign roles, agree on rules for feedback, and rehearse. Each group decides how to deliver one key line (Dev's story about the phone) and why.
Day 4: Groups perform and record. The audience notes one choice that made the dramatic irony stronger. Groups answer the reflection questions together.
Day 5: Assessment: Drama Check. Students read "The Interview" on their own and answer without AI help. Close the semester by asking students which text from the six units stayed with them, and why.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give students who are nervous about performing the stage directions reader role, or let them direct. Provide a two-column organizer (audience knows / character knows) for the essay.
- Support: allow the dramatic irony essay at 200 words with two quotations and a clear claim.
- Stretch: ask students to write a short continuation of "The Volcano" at the science fair that uses a new piece of dramatic irony, or to compare the dramatic irony in both scenes.
- Multilingual learners: readers' theater is excellent fluency practice. Let students rehearse lines with a partner first, and mark stress and pauses on their scripts. Preteach papier-mache, offstage, aside and stage directions.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit we are reading and performing short plays. Your child's group will perform a scene called "The Volcano" about a broken science project and a younger sister with a secret. Ask your child to perform a few lines for you. Watching a movie or show together? Point out a moment when you, the audience, know something a character does not, and ask your child why that makes the scene tense or funny.",
  "id": "u6-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Drama: Dialogue and Point of View",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
